newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: U.S. congressmen criticize policy on Colombia.
newsitem.headline: U.S. congressmen criticize policy on Colombia.

text.p: U.S. congressmen visiting Colombia on Monday criticised President Bill Clinton's decision to blacklist the country for its lax anti-drug efforts.

"It was my opinion that Colombia should have been certified," Representative Dennis Hastert, an Illinois Republican, told a news conference. "But there are some things that we in Congress have control over, and some things we don't."
Hastert and four other congressmen promised to press for increased anti-drug aid for Colombia on their return to Washington.
The delegation, which included one Democrat, spent three days touring the front lines of Colombia's anti-drug efforts.

Over the weekend, the congressmen witnessed the destruction of a jungle narcotics laboratory, as well as airborne drug eradication efforts in southeast Guaviare province, one of the country's main coca leaf growing regions. On Monday the group toured a recently completed anti-narcotics aviation school built with U.S. funds.

"I can now go back and tell the voters that there are thousands of people here who are not only willing to talk about the problem, but put their lives on the line every day," Representative Bob Barr, a Georgia Republican, said.
U.S.-Colombian relations sank to a new low in March after Clinton "decertified" Colombia for a second consecutive year for its failure to crack down hard enough on drug trafficking.

That meant heavy cuts in U.S. aid, but did not affect more than $80 million in anti-narcotics aid and a multi-million dollar package of drug-fighting equipment that Washington has promised Colombia this year.
The congressmen are set to leave on Tuesday morning to inspect coca leaf eradication efforts in Peru and Bolivia.
